Authority, Wealth and Halakha: The Attitude of the Sages of the 16th Century toward Doña Gracia Nasi
Authority, Wealth and Halakha: The Attitude of the Sages of the 16th Century toward Doña Gracia Nasi
The 16th century was marked by deep geopolitical and demographic upheavals in the Jewish world, which stemmed chiefly from the expulsion from Spain and Portugal and from the flow of thousands of Anusim (forced converts) back into openly professed Judaism within the Ottoman Empire and Italy [cite: 1, 2]. At the heart of this historical drama stood the figure of Doña Gracia Nasi (Beatriz de Luna Miques), whom her contemporaries called "La Señora" (the Lady) [cite: 1, 2, 3]. As a woman of immense financial wealth, worldwide diplomatic connections and extensive trade networks, she functioned in practice as the political and economic head of the Sephardic communities in the Diaspora [cite: 1, 2, 4]. The attitude of the sages of the generation toward her was complex and multidimensional; it ranged from deep admiration and unprecedented expressions of gratitude for her philanthropic and rescue work, to sharp halakhic and political confrontations over the limits of the power of secular leadership as against halakhic authority [cite: 5, 6, 7].
The Foundations of La Señora's Patronage and the Sages' Appreciation of Her
The conceptual and practical basis for the sympathetic attitude of most of the sages of the generation toward Doña Gracia derived from her central role in rehabilitating the world of Torah and the communities after the physical and spiritual devastation of the expulsion [cite: 2, 3]. Upon her open return to Judaism and her adoption of the family name "Nasi," she directed a considerable part of her wealth to the establishment of religious and communal institutions [cite: 3]. She founded yeshivot, synagogues and hospitals in Constantinople and in other Jewish centers, and thereby became the direct patroness of many Torah scholars and halakhic decisors who were supported at her table [cite: 3]. Strong evidence of her unique standing among the spiritual leadership is the fact that a synagogue she established in Izmir was called simply "La Señora" (the Lady), with no need to mention her explicit name – a clear expression of the reverence and the unchallenged authority she enjoyed in the eyes of the community's sages and its leaders [cite: 3].
In addition, the sages of the generation viewed favorably her cultural initiatives, which were intended to bring the returning Anusim closer to their religion. Projects such as her financial support for the publication of the "Ferrara Bible" in a Ladino translation in 1553 served as a primary educational and halakhic tool for those Jews who had lost their knowledge of the Hebrew language under the yoke of persecution [cite: 3]. Her influence extended beyond the borders of the Middle East; already during her stay in Europe, she conducted complex dealings with the authorities and used her wealth to assist the Anusim legally and financially [cite: 1, 3]. Among other things, she obtained the Pope's permission to transfer the remains of her late husband, Francisco Mendes, for Jewish burial on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem – a step that was highly esteemed by the sages of the Land of Israel, who saw in it halakhic and familial self-sacrifice [cite: 1].
The Ancona Boycott: The Watershed in Relations with the Rabbinic Establishment
The formative event in which the attitude of the sages of the generation toward Doña Gracia was put to the test, and which exposed the structural and legitimate split within the world of halakha, was the "Ancona Boycott" in 1556 [cite: 5, 8]. The port city of Ancona, which was under the rule of the Papal States, had served for years as a safe haven for Portuguese Anusim thanks to the attractive policy of Popes Clement III and Paul III, who granted them protection and trading rights [cite: 6]. However, with the accession of Pope Paul IV in 1555, the policy changed completely: harsh decrees were imposed, a ghetto was established, and the tribunal of the Inquisition began to persecute the Anusim who had returned to Judaism [cite: 6]. The climax of the antisemitic wave was the burning at the stake of 25 Portuguese Anusim, on charges of heresy and of returning to Judaism, in April 1556 [cite: 4, 6, 8].
In response to this tragedy, Doña Gracia, together with her nephew Don Joseph Nasi, initiated a step unprecedented in Jewish history: an organized economic boycott by Jewish merchants against the port of Ancona, and the rerouting of all maritime trade routes to the nearby port of Pesaro [cite: 5, 6, 8]. Doña Gracia, who took care to act within the accepted framework of the law, understood that in order to ensure the success of the boycott, binding halakhic legitimacy was needed [cite: 6]. She sent her personal representative, Rabbi Yehuda Faraj, to present her position before the great rabbis of Italy and the Ottoman Empire in order to enlist their halakhic support for the boycott [cite: 6]. At the same time, she exercised her influence at the court of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, who sent an official letter of protest to the Pope demanding the release of the prisoners who enjoyed Ottoman protection [cite: 6].
Doña Gracia's appeal created a deep rift and an unprecedented halakhic controversy among the decisors, who were divided over the question of authority, effectiveness and the dangers inherent in a unilateral boycott [cite: 5].
Rabbi Yosef ibn Lev (Maharival), one of the great sages of Constantinople, stood firmly at Doña Gracia's side [cite: 7]. He signed the boycott and issued a precedent-setting halakhic ruling according to which a community has full legal authority to compel its members to comply with a decision, while applying severe internal sanctions against those who violate it [cite: 7]. Their close cooperation was also expressed in the fact that Maharival signed a special ban of excommunication (cherem) against a man who had informed the authorities about Don Joseph Nasi, her partner in leadership [cite: 7]. This attitude reflected a rabbinic conception that saw Doña Gracia's leadership as a legitimate political arm of the Jewish people in a time of crisis [cite: 6].
By contrast, Rabbi Shmuel de Medina (Maharashdam) of Salonica, along with other sages in Italy, firmly opposed the boycott [cite: 5, 7]. His halakhic responsa, published later in the collections of his rulings, expressed the heavy concern that halting trade with Ancona would arouse the Pope's wrath and bring about the expulsion or massacre of the other Jewish communities in the Papal States [cite: 5, 9]. The opponents of the boycott argued that private merchants could not be forced to endanger their source of livelihood and to damage their relations with the authorities in the name of abstract solidarity [cite: 5]. This debate underscored that while the sages appreciated Doña Gracia's moral motives, some of them refused to subordinate the security considerations of the local communities to the broad political and economic strategy that she had charted [cite: 5, 6]. In the end, owing to the absence of halakhic consensus and the opposition of the merchants, the boycott failed and the Anusim who remained in Ancona were not saved [cite: 3, 8].
The Tiberias Enterprise: The Encounter between Political Vision and Religious Aspiration
An additional dimension that illuminates the sages' complex attitude toward Doña Gracia is her vision for the settlement of the Land of Israel [cite: 4]. After leasing the Tiberias region from Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, Doña Gracia aspired to turn the ruined city into a thriving economic, industrial and Torah center [cite: 4, 10]. The plan was based on developing a local silk and wool industry and on opening the city's gates to absorb refugees and Anusim from Europe [cite: 10].
The sages saw in this initiative a historical and religious step of immense spiritual importance. Although the economic vision of Doña Gracia and Don Joseph Nasi was not fully realized before their deaths (Doña Gracia died in Constantinople in 1569 and Don Joseph in 1579), and the attempt was revived only temporarily and on a limited scale by Shlomo ben Yaish, the rabbinic attitude toward the undertaking was highly positive [cite: 10]. The leaders of the communities saw in her efforts to renew the settlement in Tiberias a first, tangible expression of processes of physical redemption [cite: 4]. The very combination of private capital, government patronage and an infrastructure for Torah study was encouraged by the sages, who saw in her a leader working not only for material welfare but also for the fulfillment of the commandment of settling the Land [cite: 4].
Her Legacy and Historical Memory in Halakhic Literature and Antiquity
Doña Gracia's exceptional gender status in the traditional Jewish society of the 16th century posed a complex challenge to the world of halakha, which was patriarchal at its foundation [cite: 1, 2]. Nevertheless, the historical analysis of the documentation shows that the sages of the generation chose to relate to her out of deep appreciation for her authority and her practical power, and not out of a paternalistic approach that belittled her work because she was a woman [cite: 2, 6].
In the literature of the generation and in later historical books, such as the book "Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah" (Chain of Tradition), Doña Gracia is described with extreme admiration as a figure of rare courage, extraordinary leadership ability and uncompromising devotion to the defense of her Jewish brothers [cite: 6]. The sages of the generation understood that in an era of persecution and political instability, her wealth and diplomatic influence were vital to the physical survival of the Torah institutions and the communities [cite: 3, 4].
The halakhic controversies that revolved around her political decisions were not intended to challenge her leadership as such, but to examine their practical implications for the security of innocent people [cite: 5]. In the end, the attitude of the sages of the 16th century toward Doña Gracia Nasi attests that she was perceived as a senior and indispensable partner in the spiritual leadership, with whom they steered the Jewish ship through one of the stormiest and most challenging periods the Sephardic Diaspora ever knew [cite: 2, 5].

A Crown of Leadership and a Doctrine of Kindness: The Political Work, the Torah Contribution and the Legacy of Doña Gracia Nasi
This survey presents the fascinating life story of Doña Gracia Nasi, an exemplary figure who led the Jewish people in the 16th century, combining rare economic power with political vision. The text traces the transition of "the Señora" from a life of concealment as a Jewish woman forced to convert in Portugal to the management of a worldwide financial empire, which she used as a tool for rescuing refugees and fortifying the world of Torah. The pillars of the article deal with her daring initiatives, foremost among them the leadership of a political commercial boycott, the first of its kind, and a groundbreaking attempt to renew Jewish sovereignty in Tiberias. The purpose of the source is to restore to public awareness the legacy of a woman who was ahead of her time, and to examine how her philanthropic and national influence is today enjoying a renewal through academic research and state commemoration in the State of Israel.
A Crown of Leadership and a Doctrine of Kindness: The Political Work, the Torah Contribution and the Legacy of Doña Gracia Nasi
Introduction: A Portrait of Leadership in Secret and in the Open
Doña Gracia Nasi (1510–1569), also known by her Christian names Beatriz de Luna Miques and Gracia Mendes, and by her Hebrew name Chana Gershiya Nasi, is considered one of the most influential and daring leadership figures in Jewish history at the beginning of the early modern period [cite: 1]. She was born in Lisbon, Portugal, to a distinguished family of Anusim who had fled from Castile in the wake of the expulsion from Spain in 1492 [cite: 1]. Her parents, Aloro de Luna and Filipa Mendes Benveniste, were forced to undergo compulsory baptism into Christianity in 1497 together with the rest of the Jews of Portugal, and led a double life of secretly observing the commandments [cite: 1]. Only when she reached the age of bat mitzvah was the secret of her Jewish identity revealed to her, an event that shaped her worldview and impelled her to devote her life, her wealth and her public standing to the rescue of her people, to the redemption of captives, to the fortification of the world of Torah and to the establishment of an independent national entity in the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 2, 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Financial Empire of the House of Mendes and Benveniste
In 1528 Doña Gracia was betrothed to her uncle, Francisco Mendes, whose Hebrew name was Tzemach Benveniste [cite: 1]. Francisco headed a thriving international trading house that dealt in silver and spices, and especially in black pepper, which was under the exclusive control of the Portuguese royal institution "House of India" [cite: 1]. The marriage was conducted in two ceremonies: a secret Jewish ceremony in the cellar of their home and a public Christian ceremony in a church [cite: 1]. The family's immense wealth and its decisive economic role in Portugal served as armor and protection for them against the persecutions of the Portuguese Inquisition in those days [cite: 1].
Upon the death of Francisco Mendes in 1536, Doña Gracia inherited half of the family fortune and took upon herself the management of the business alongside her brother-in-law, Diogo Mendes (Hebrew name: Meir Benveniste), who ran the bank's branch in Antwerp [cite: 1]. Because of the growing threats of the Inquisition in Portugal, Doña Gracia was forced to flee to Antwerp together with her only daughter Ana-Reina, her younger sister Brianda de Luna, and her cousin João Miques, who later became known by his Jewish name Don Joseph Nasi [cite: 1].
After the death of Diogo Mendes in 1543, his will appointed Doña Gracia as chief manager of the family's business and banking conglomerate [cite: 1]. In 1544 the family moved to Venice, where Doña Gracia became embroiled in a bitter inheritance dispute with her sister Brianda (who had married Diogo in 1539) [cite: 1]. In 1549 Duke Ercole II of the House of Este granted the family safe haven in Ferrara and recognized her inheritance rights, and thereby opened before her the gate to return to her Judaism openly and to use the historic family name "Nasi" [cite: 1, 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Geographic Stations and the Economic-Political Activity
Doña Gracia's activity spread across the main centers of power of Europe and the Ottoman Empire, as she exploited the trade and influence routes of the Mendes bank to advance national and spiritual goals [cite: 1, 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Two-Tier Rescue Strategy: The Physical and Spiritual Rehabilitation of the Anusim of Spain and Portugal
Doña Gracia Nasi's philanthropic work was characterized by a long-term systemic vision, which combined an immediate physical response to the distress of the refugees with spiritual and cultural solutions intended to prevent their assimilation and the loss of their Jewish identity [cite: 3].
Physical Rescue and the Redemption of Captives
Doña Gracia operated a far-reaching smuggling network that crossed political borders [cite: 3]. Her commercial agents throughout Europe exploited the passage of the bank's goods to hide Anusim, to issue them forged documents and to bribe customs officials and guards [cite: 1, 3]. She invested vast sums in the redemption of Jewish captives who had been seized by pirates in the Mediterranean or arrested by the Christian authorities [cite: 2, 3].
As part of her efforts to protect refugees, Doña Gracia did not hesitate to use her direct political influence with the rulers of Europe; among other things, she paid the enormous sum of 1,000 gold ducats to Sigismund II Augustus, King of Poland, in order to secure the freedom and security of Jewish refugees who had been settled in his kingdom [cite: 1].
Spiritual Rehabilitation and the Ferrara Bible (1553)
Alongside the physical rescue, Doña Gracia identified that the long years of forced conversion had created a deep spiritual rupture [cite: 3]. Many Anusim who returned to the fold of Judaism no longer mastered the Hebrew language and could not read the sacred writings, which were accessible at that time almost solely in Latin or in dubious Christian versions [cite: 3]. To fill this cultural and religious void, Doña Gracia financed the printing of foundational Jewish books in the local languages of the Iberian Peninsula [cite: 3].
The central achievement of this enterprise was the printing of the "Ferrara Bible" in 1553, a monumental translation of the Bible into Judeo-Spanish [cite: 1, 3]. The project was carried out by the printer Abraham Usque and the translator Yom Tov ben Levi Athias [cite: 1, 3]. The Bible was characterized by an extreme and literal adherence to the structure of the Hebrew sentence, which gave it the air of an archaic Ladino in Latin letters [cite: 3]. This translation scrupulously avoided traditional Christian interpretations [cite: 3].
Bibliographical studies, foremost among them the comprehensive study of Prof. Stanley Rypins in the 20th century, which examined 49 copies of the work, revealed the theological dispute surrounding the translation of the word "almah" in the Book of Isaiah (7:14) [cite: 3]. Whereas the Christian Church consistently translated this word as "virgin" (virgen) in order to support its religious dogma, in the Jewish version of the Ferrara Bible, which was officially dedicated to Doña Gracia Nasi, the printers chose to leave the original word in Latin letters (Alma) or to translate it as moca (a young woman), in order to prevent foreign theological distortions [cite: 1, 3].
Doña Gracia's economic and spiritual contribution was commemorated in a magnificent poetic dedication at the opening of the book, which extols her work as an agent of spiritual rescue [cite: 3]. In the same year, the epic Portuguese work of Samuel Usque, "Consolation for the Tribulations of Israel" (Nechama le-Tlaot Yisrael), also enjoyed her patronage and the beginning of its printing, with the author calling her "the heart within the body" of the broken community of the Anusim [cite: 1].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Her Torah Doctrine and the Network of Patronage in Constantinople and Izmir
Doña Gracia Nasi's Torah doctrine was not formulated in theoretical writings or in collections of responsa, but was expressed in practice in the building of a broad institutional Torah infrastructure and in the consolidation of the world of halakha among the communities of the expelled and the returnees [cite: 1, 2]. Upon her arrival in Constantinople in 1553, she founded yeshivot, synagogues, study halls and hospitals [cite: 1, 2].
Her public conception held that without strong institutions of learning and direct financial support for Torah scholars, the refugee communities could not rehabilitate their spiritual lives [cite: 1, 3]. She granted regular stipends to rabbinic scholars and prominent rabbis, and helped them publish their works [cite: 1].
A living testimony to her unprecedented standing among Sephardic Jewry is the synagogue she established in the city of Izmir, which was called "La Señora" (the Lady) [cite: 1]. The fact that an entire Jewish community named a central house of prayer after her general title alone, without needing to mention her explicit name, constitutes rare historical evidence of her unchallenged influence and her informal spiritual and public authority in the Jewish world of the 16th century [cite: 1].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Ancona Boycott: A Halakhic, Economic and Political Conflict
In 1555 a dramatic turn occurred in the attitude of the Papal State toward the Anusim; Pope Paul IV issued a harsh bull against the "hidden Jews" [cite: 1, 5]. In 1556, in the port city of Ancona, the Pope ordered the arrest of dozens of Portuguese Anusim who had returned to Judaism, confiscated their property and burned 24 of them at the stake (23 men and one woman) on charges of heresy and of returning to the religion of their fathers [cite: 1, 5]. Among those executed was Jacob Musso, Doña Gracia's chief business agent in the city [cite: 1, 5].
The diplomatic attempts to save the prisoners failed, and in response Doña Gracia and Don Joseph Nasi initiated a bold and unprecedented step: the "Ancona Boycott" [cite: 1, 5]. They convened the sages of Constantinople and declared a comprehensive Jewish commercial boycott of the port of Ancona [cite: 1, 5]. Ships owned or controlled by Jewish merchants were ordered to divert their route and sail to the port of Pesaro in the Duchy of Urbino, whose ruler, Duke Guidobaldo II, agreed to absorb the surviving refugees on condition that Ottoman trade be directed to his port [cite: 5].
This initiative aroused a bitter controversy that tore apart the world of halakha and the rabbinate in the Ottoman Empire and in Italy, as emerges from the responsa literature of the period [cite: 1, 5].
In the end, the absence of a central authority with real enforcement power over all the scattered communities prevented the boycott's success [cite: 5]. Many Jewish merchants, among them merchants of the Bursa community, refused to obey the boycott order because of the infrastructural limitations of the port of Pesaro and because the boycott harmed their personal livelihood [cite: 5]. With the death of Pope Paul IV the boycott faded away entirely, but it remained in history as a dramatic landmark, the first attempt to use collective economic power as a political weapon for the defense of Jews [cite: 1, 5].
The consequences of the economic and political crisis also reached the printing houses of the period [cite: 3]. The printing house of Abraham Usque in Ferrara, which printed in 1556 the book of laments "Shiltei ha-Giborim" (Shields of the Heroes) by Rabbi Jacob of Fano (which included a lament over the death of the 24 martyrs of Ancona), drew the attention of Bishop Antonio Ghislieri (later Pope Pius V) [cite: 3]. Ghislieri ordered the book burned and Usque punished, which led to the final closure of the famous printing house in 1558 [cite: 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Tiberias Enterprise: Territorial Sovereignty and Coping with Messianic Visions
In 1561 Doña Gracia and her nephew Don Joseph Nasi (who married her daughter Ana-Reina in 1553) approached Sultan Suleiman I with a request to lease cities in the Land of Israel [cite: 1]. At first they sought to lease Jerusalem, but after the Ottoman authorities refused, they leased the city of Tiberias and its surroundings for an annual payment of 1,000 gold ducats [cite: 1, 2, 4].
The Tiberias enterprise was intended to constitute a sovereign and practical solution to the plight of the Jews of the Diaspora and the Anusim of Europe [cite: 1, 2, 4]. The economic and social plan that Doña Gracia drew up comprised several central components:
Physical construction: rebuilding the ruined city walls and erecting new houses in order to absorb waves of immigration [cite: 1, 2, 4].
Industrial development: planting thousands of mulberry trees and importing silkworms in order to develop a thriving local silk industry that would provide stable and independent sources of employment, instead of relying on charity funds [cite: 1].
Spiritual and political center: building a magnificent palace for Doña Gracia herself, who was preparing to move to live in the city in the summer of 1566 [cite: 1, 6]. The Portuguese traveler Pantaleão de Aveiro, who visited the Land of Israel at that time, documented the enormous excitement and the anticipation of the Jews of the Land at the arrival of "the rich Portuguese lady" [cite: 1].
This enterprise aroused intense messianic hopes throughout the Jewish world [cite: 1]. The renewed settlement in a holy city was seen by many as part of the approaching process of redemption [cite: 1]. However, this messianic ferment aroused deep concern among the leaders of the generation and the rabbis [cite: 1]. The 16th century was characterized by a proliferation of false messiahs, who not infrequently led their followers to spiritual disorientation, to bitter disappointment and even to mass conversion to Christianity or Islam [cite: 1].
The cautious leadership saw in Doña Gracia's powerful and beloved public image a source of risk that could easily turn into an uncontrolled messianic focal point [cite: 1]. This concern led to a clear tendency to downplay her work and to silence her legacy after her death in 1569 [cite: 1]. Her premature death prevented her from realizing her dream of actually going up to Tiberias, and in the absence of her dominant leadership the settlement enterprise in Tiberias faded away [cite: 1]. The historical fear of a messianic outbreak caused her figure to be largely omitted from the traditional historical consciousness of later generations [cite: 1].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Transition from Oblivion to State and Cultural Commemoration in the State of Israel
For hundreds of years Doña Gracia remained a forgotten figure on the margins of modern Zionist historiography, which tended to focus on the state-building and pioneering enterprises of the 18th and 19th centuries while ignoring the early attempts at sovereignty of the 16th century [cite: 1]. Only in the late 20th century and the early 21st century did an accelerated trend of rediscovery, academic research and state commemoration of her legacy begin [cite: 1].
The most comprehensive academic historical research on her life was written by Dr. Tzvika Sachayik, who carried out a detailed doctoral dissertation funded by the Doña Gracia Association headed by the businessman Yaakov Amsalem [cite: 1, 7]. This research served as the basis for many commemoration and cultural initiatives in the State of Israel [cite: 1].
Cultural Institutions, Tourism and State Events
The House of Doña Gracia: In Tiberias a hotel and a living museum, unique of its kind, was established at 3 HaPerachim Street, serving as a cultural center for empowering women's leadership and fostering the heritage of Ladino and Sephardic Jewry [cite: 1, 6, 8, 9]. The place is designed in the style of the palace of the Renaissance lady and offers interactive exhibits that simulate a journey in time into her life [cite: 6, 9, 10].
The Doña Gracia Festival and Observation Point: An annual festival was established in her memory beginning in the year of the 500th anniversary of her birth [cite: 1]. At the same time, the Association planted a grove north of the Switzerland Forest overlooking the Kinneret, called "Doña Gracia Observation Point," in which a commemorative rock telling the story of her life was placed [cite: 1].
State Commemoration: To mark 500 years since her birth, a special state ceremony was held at the President's Residence on the initiative of the Doña Gracia Association and with the encouragement of Israel Prize laureate Geula Cohen [cite: 1]. The event was attended by the President of the State, the President of the Supreme Court and former Minister of Education Gideon Sa'ar, who worked to integrate the figure and legacy of Doña Gracia into the official curriculum of the Ministry of Education [cite: 1, 11]. In addition, the Israeli Company for Medals and Coins issued an official medal in her memory [cite: 1].
Naming of Streets: Streets named after her were designated in the cities of Tiberias, Haifa and Netanya, as part of a trend of bringing the heritage of women leaders of Sephardic Jewry into the public space in Israel [cite: 2].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Doña Gracia's Representations in Literature and Theater
Her stormy and eventful life story has inspired writers, playwrights and historians over the years, who have tried to fathom the character of the richest Jewish leader of the Renaissance world [cite: 1, 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary and Historical Assessment
The leadership of Doña Gracia Nasi presents a unique model of leadership that combines wealth, international diplomacy, a spiritual-Torah orientation and a political vision ahead of its time [cite: 1, 2]. In a period when women were almost entirely absent from public decision-making centers, Doña Gracia succeeded in steering one of the world's great financial empires, in establishing a physical and spiritual shield for tens of thousands of Anusim, in heading international halakhic and political struggles, and in laying the first cornerstone for the attempts at the sovereign return of the Jewish people to its land [cite: 1, 3, 5].
Despite the historical attempts to silence her legacy out of fear of extreme messianic movements, Doña Gracia's return to the forefront of the public and scholarly stage in the modern State of Israel attests to the growing recognition of her historical importance and of her centrality as a foremost Zionist pioneer [cite: 1, 7].
